chunks: How a DAC works. The question: How does a DAC work?
A DAC (digital-to-analog converter) turns a binary number into a voltage. It is the opposite of an ADC. Each bit of the number switches on a share of the reference voltage.
The top bit adds half, the next adds a quarter, and so on, and the shares are added together.
Imagine mixing a drink from measuring cups. There is a cup worth 1/2 liter, one worth 1/4, one worth 1/8. Each bit of the number is a yes-or-no instruction: pour this cup or not.
The total in the jug is the output. The code 101 means pour the half and the eighth cups. Even with every cup poured, the jug holds 7/8 of a liter: one smallest cup short of full.
Each node has a 2R leg driven by a bit.

Looking to the right of any node, the rest of the ladder is always 2R (for example R in series with 2R 2R ), so each node sees R to ground, so the ladder halves each bit's effect as it propagates toward the output (left).
The LSB end is terminated by a 2R to ground.
Code: the binary number you give the DAC. Reference voltage: ("How an ADC works"): the voltage that sets the full-scale size of the output.
LSB: the smallest step of the output, the reference divided by 2 to the N . R-2R ladder: a network of resistors with values R and 2R that divides voltage into the binary shares.
Reconstruction filter: a filter that removes the sharp steps and turns the staircase output into a smooth voltage.
Take a 3-bit DAC with a 3. 3 volts reference. There are 2 to the 3 equals 8 codes, so one step is 3. 3 / 8, about 0. 41 volts. Code 0 gives 0 volts.
Code 5 (binary 101) gives 5 times 0. 4125 volts, about 2. 06 volts. The biggest code, 7, gives about 2. 89 volts, one step short of 3. 3 volts.
The output between updates is a staircase, so it usually needs a buffer (an amplifier that copies the voltage so a load cannot pull it down) and a filter. That is the whole idea.
"A DAC turns an N-bit code into a voltage, V ref times code over 2 to the N , by summing binary-weighted contributions: the MSB is half the reference, the next a quarter, and so on.
The classic circuit is an R-2R ladder: two resistor values, and the ladder to the right of every node looks like 2R, so each bit's contribution halves per stage.
The output resistance is R, so you buffer it with an op-amp, and the staircase output is smoothed by a low-pass filter.
Alternatives are binary-weighted, resistor-string, current-steering and PWM plus an RC filter."
